product.title: Double Heavyweight Crewneck T-Shirt - White
product.body_html:
We got in on Wonder Looper before the brand had a website. The owners asked whether we wanted some of the heaviest knits being made anywhere, and that is a short conversation. Heavyweight tees are familiar ground for us and for most of the people who shop here, but these sit in a different category. The jersey runs 409gsm, or 12.1oz per square yard, roughly double what the industry calls heavyweight, and the surprise is that it still drapes. A fabric this dense could easily hang like cardboard. Instead, the weight pulls it down into a clean line off the shoulders. Knitting it this way takes time. The jersey is circular knit in Japan at low tension, which is where the uneven surface texture comes from, the kind of irregular face that makes a vintage tee look like a vintage tee rather than a printed blank. Construction holds up its end. The collar is a binder neck with ribbing, bound rather than simply set in, so it keeps its shape through years of pulling the shirt over your head. The side seams are joined on a union special flat seam machine, which butts the panels together and stitches them flat so there is no ridge running down your ribs. Cut and sewn in Japan. We were one of the first shops in the country to carry these. They sold out, we reordered, and they sold out again.

product.title: Zip Hoodie - Double Heavyweight French Terry - Navy
product.body_html:
Wakayama sits at the center of Japan's knitting industry, and it is where this French terry is made, run on circular knitting machines at a low 10 gauge. Fewer needles around the cylinder means heavier yarn and a coarser, more irregular surface, and it means the knitting takes its time. What comes off the machine lands at roughly twice the weight of a standard heavyweight knit, with large, soft loops covering the entire inside face. From there, the interior is lightly brushed, just enough to puff those loops into a half-fleece that holds warmth close while leaving the terry structure intact, so the inside reads fuller and softer and still looks like the knit it is. The finished garment is rinse-washed and pre-shrunk to settle the fabric and keep further shrinkage at home to a minimum. Raglan sleeves let the shoulders move freely under all that weight, and ribbed panels run down the sides into the cuffs and hem to give the knit structure and hold its shape. Flat-seam construction keeps the joins smooth against the skin and gives the piece a clean, finished look throughout. Down the front runs a heavy-gauge two-way Waldes zipper, a name that traces back to the early decades of the zipper trade, and the two-way slider lets the hem open up while the top stays closed. A drawstring hood and split hand-warmer pockets complete the front.

The shell handled wind and weather, and a separate liner buttoned inside it to handle warmth, which meant a soldier could add or drop insulation as conditions changed. Collectors figured out decades ago that the liner works perfectly well on its own, and orSlow takes that idea the rest of the way, building the Fish Tail Liner as a standalone jacket rather than a component. The neckline is collarless, so nothing fights a scarf or the collar of whatever goes over it, and the front closes with buttons. Two large patch pockets sit at the hips. product.title: 01-6155-52 - Suede Touch Classic Coveralls - Coffee Brown
product.body_html:
In thirteen years of doing this, we have never handled a fabric quite like this one. Faux suede has its roots in Japan, where mills worked out how to split polyester into filaments finer than silk and brush them up into a nap that reads like leather at a glance. The fabric on this coverall comes out of that lineage and then goes somewhere stranger. It looks like suede and behaves like a technical cloth, carrying a stiffness much closer to raw denim, so the jacket stands away from the body and holds its own lines rather than falling soft against you. That structure is the whole point here. It also shrugs off water and asks for none of the careful handling real suede demands, which makes it a jacket you can actually wear in weather. orSlow builds it on its coverall pattern with an A-line silhouette that widens as it falls, and the brand's own buttons and sleeve design handle the details that make it recognizable from across a room. Four rounded pockets break up the front, three of them patch pockets and one a flap pocket, with brass snaps running up the placket and an internal locker loop at the neck. It works across three seasons and settles in nicely the longer you wear it.

product.title: 03-0013N-W61 - Waffle Long Sleeve T-Shirt - Black
product.body_html:
Waffle knits earn their place in cold weather through geometry. The honeycomb structure raises and recesses the surface into hundreds of small pockets, and each one holds a little air against the body, which is why waffle insulates while still breathing freely and why it spent a century as the standard for thermal underwear before anyone wore it on the outside. orSlow knits this one in Japan at 5.8oz with a soft hand and a good amount of give, helped along by the single percent of polyurethane blended into the cotton body, which lets the knit stretch as you move and return to shape afterward. The texture is the point as much as the warmth here, breaking up the surface of an outfit in a way a flat jersey leaves alone. Ribbing finishes the collar and the sleeve ends in 100% cotton. One thing worth knowing before the first wash: the fabric is not pre-rinsed, so orSlow expects roughly 3 to 4% shrinkage, which works out to about half an inch to an inch across most dimensions and a little more through the length.

Dye behaves differently depending on when it meets the cloth. Rogue Territory sends this 11oz Japanese selvedge canvas through a roll dye in its raw state, which lays the brown onto the surface of the yarns rather than driving it all the way to the core. That is the same principle behind a good pair of raw jeans, and it sets the shirt up to shed pigment slowly, lightening at the elbows, the cuffs, the placket, and anywhere else the fabric moves against itself. The dyeing happens in Los Angeles, a short trip from the floor where the shirts are sewn. Once construction is finished, each piece goes through an industrial wash that pulls some of the surface dye back off, so the shirt arrives with a worn-in patina already started and a hand that has lost its stiffness. The wash also means the brown stays where it belongs, so you can wear it over anything. Inside, contrast red chain stitching runs the seams and ties back to the bold red selvedge ID, and the placket is cut on the selvedge so that finished edge faces out every time the shirt is open. The canvas carries a natural stretch that lets it relax into shape quickly. Dual chest pockets, triple-needle chainstitched seams with run-off, a herringbone locker loop, and antiqued brass snaps handle the rest.

product.title: Classic Cardigan - Pewter Alpaca
product.body_html:
Alpacas come in two types, and the difference shows up in the fleece. Huacaya fleece grows with a crimp that gives it loft and a woolly look, while Suri fleece grows in long, straight locks that hang down the animal in ropes, closer to dreadlocks than to a sheep's coat. Those uncrimped fibers take light differently, which is where Suri gets its luster, and spun into yarn they leave a halo of fine hairs standing off the surface. Suri alpacas account for roughly 10% of the world's alpaca population, so the fleece is harder to come by and prized by the people who work with it. 3sixteen knits this season's Classic Cardigan from a Suri alpaca and wool blend in pewter, and the character of the fiber carries the piece: light and airy in the hand, hairy and textured across the surface, with a quiet sheen running through the color. product.body_html:
Before automated sewing machines took over the factory floor and rivets became the standard answer to a stress point, a pair of work pants got its strength from the hands that built it and the stitches those hands put down. The 900HM-60XX is ONI's reconstruction of that approach, and the HM in the name stands for handmade. Rows of stitching pile up where a later pair would simply place a rivet, the seams are flat-felled rather than chainstitched lap seams, the bar tacks run linear, and the belt loops are the Banzai type, named for the way their raised ends look like arms thrown up in celebration. Every one of those choices slows the sewing down and leaves the finished pair with the slightly irregular, squared-off character of old workwear. The fabric looks back to American denim of the 1960s, woven and finished in Japan at 12oz with an uneven surface, subtle slub running through it, and the visual depth ONI has built its name on. That weight keeps the jeans wearable deep into warm weather while giving up none of the texture, and the irregularity of the weave means the fades will land differently on every pair.

product.title: Denime "Lot. 224" 66 Model Mother Cotton 14oz Straight Jeans Natural
product.body_html:
No indigo, no dye, no finishing. The Lot 224-66M takes Denime’s reproduction of the 1966 model — the late-sixties American jean that sits at the heart of the brand’s XX Series — and cuts it from cloth that has been left exactly as it came off the loom. The fabric is Kurabo Mother Cotton, a 7.3 × 7.3 count selvedge developed with the Okayama mill from a blend that includes natural brown cotton, which gives the ecru its warmth. It is woven on a GL3 shuttle loom and goes through none of the usual rope dyeing, so what you see is the true construction of an XX denim: the uneven yarn, the slub, the hairy surface, in the color of the cotton itself.

At 14oz the cloth has real body, and because it is unsanforized and sold loomstate — unwashed — it will shrink to size in the first soak and then do what a living fabric does: soften, crease, and pick up the marks of wear and washing as a patina of its own, without the contrast of indigo to lean on.

The pattern reproduces the sewing specifications of the 1966 model and its silhouette: a straight leg with a mid rise and regular volume from the thigh to the hem, the easiest of the vintage cuts to wear every day. Details follow the period — an iron button fly, 100% cotton thread, copper rivets, a paper patch with the Denime logo and a white and yellow selvedge ID. Denime has been making jeans like this since 1988, as one of the Osaka Five. 100% cotton. Made in Japan.

Fit Notes: Denime remains faithful to non-washed, unsanforized (loomstate) denim, so it’s important to note that these jeans will shrink. We highly recommend soaking the jeans in warm water before first wear. Expect approximately 4 cm (1.5") of shrinkage in the waist and 7.5 cm (3") in the inseam after soaking, so please refer to the product size chart accordingly. This model fits true to size after shrinkage, meaning the tagged size closely matches the actual waist measurement once the shrinkage has occurred. Compared to most global American brands, sizing is similar, so you can take your usual size. product.title: Samurai Jeans S310XX19ozII 19oz Super Wide Jeans

The fabric is Samurai’s 19oz selvedge, and the construction is worth understanding. The warp is a No. 5 uneven slub yarn spun from coarse, hard raw cotton with a high-twist method that deliberately pushes the surface toward rough and grainy; slub in a yarn this thick is hard to make look natural, and here it comes through as organic irregularity rather than a forced effect. The weft is a thick No. 4 yarn, which leaves the inside of the fabric softer against the skin while the outer face stays coarse and heavy. Firm in hand, it is built for high-contrast fades, and it comes one-washed.

The cut is a super wide straight with a deep, high rise (32 cm / 12.6" at the front on a 32), a very roomy top block and a leg that runs wide and straight to a 26 cm (10.2") opening. For all that width, the proportions have been drawn to avoid exaggeration: it reads as a wide jean, not a costume.

Unsanforized, 100% cotton, made in Japan.

product.title: Samurai Jeans S0710XX-BOB 15oz "Aoki Tachikage" Black On Blue Slim Straight Jeans
product.body_html:
Aoki Tachikage — 青き太刀影, “Blue Blade Shadow” — is the image of a sword cutting through darkness and leaving a blue glint behind it, and the denim is built to do exactly that. On the hanger these jeans read as black-on-black. With wear they turn out to be two colors: the black is the surface, and the blue is what it was hiding.

The fabric works in layers. The warp is a #6 slub yarn that is first rope-dyed in indigo and then overdyed with sulphur black, a three-stage process that leaves black on top, indigo underneath and the natural white core at the center. As the pair breaks in, the sulphur black wears off the high points first, exposing the indigo; the indigo then fades in its own time toward the white core, so every worn area eventually shows three tones at once — black, exposed blue, and the pale core of the yarn. The weft is an uneven #6 yarn dyed sulphur black as well, which deepens the overall tone and fades to grey rather than white. At 15oz, the cloth has enough body to crease hard and hold the contrast, and the silver lamé selvedge — the brand’s nod to the samurai’s blade — runs the outseam.

The 710 is Samurai’s slim straight: a mid rise, a slim thigh and a leg that runs straight with a slight taper to a 19.5 cm (7.7") opening — the trimmest frame in the lineup for a fabric that fades this hard.

The details were drawn for this denim alone: a five-button fly in blue-coated metal embossed with the Samurai name, navy sewing thread throughout, jacquard pocket bags woven with a family-crest pattern, a selvedge-cut coin pocket and the brand’s goatskin leather patch. The denim is unsanforized and one-washed. 100% cotton. Made in Japan.

product.title: Mooncastle Shetland Wool Crewneck Pullover Gold
product.body_html:
Shetland wool has always traded softness for character: a lofty, slightly hairy fiber with real warmth and the kind of durability that keeps a sweater in service for decades. Mooncastle's SW1 keeps that character and rounds off its edge by knitting the Shetland together with merino in an exclusive 100% wool blend — the body and resilience of the one, the softer hand of the other, in a fabric that feels light on the shoulders and holds heat the way a proper Shetland should.

The sweater is made by seamless whole-garment knitting: the body and sleeves come off the machine as a single piece, with no seams at the shoulders or sides to bulk up, rub, or give way. The result is a clean crew neck with ribbed cuffs and hem and an even drape all round. Gold is one of ten colors in the range, sitting between mustard and ochre, and it is a shade that reads well against denim and dark tailoring alike. As with all knitwear, allow a variation of 1–2 cm between pieces.

Mooncastle recommends dry cleaning; tumble drying and machine washing will shrink and distort the wool. Between wears, a soft brush keeps the surface tidy, any pills should be removed with a pill comb rather than pulled, and a day's rest after a day's wear will add years to the sweater. Made in Japan.

Fit Notes: This sweater follows Japanese sizing and runs a bit small. Compared to most global American brands, we recommend sizing up one from your usual size for a comfortable fit — an L fits similarly to an American M. The knit is light and close to the body, with ribbed cuffs and hem that hold with a moderate grip, and knitwear can vary by 1–2 cm from piece to piece. As always, we strongly recommend checking our size chart and comparing it with your best-fitting garment to ensure the right fit.

product.body_html:
A crew neck reduced to what matters. Mooncastle, the Osaka knitwear house, makes this sweater from 100% superfine Australian merino — the finest grade of the fiber, which is why the surface has a soft sheen and a smooth, almost silky hand, and why it sits against bare skin with little of the itch coarser wool brings. It is knitted in a 12-gauge plain jersey: fine enough to go under a jacket or over a shirt without bulk, dense enough to hold real warmth and to last.

The shape is drawn to be worn, not noticed. Ribbed cuffs and hem hold with a moderate grip rather than pinching, and the body follows the torso in a clean line that works with tailoring as easily as with jeans and sneakers. Beige melange — a heathered, undyed-looking tone — was a color Mooncastle sold last year only in its own stores and at select Japanese stockists; it is now offered while stock lasts.

Care is simpler than most merino: machine washable on a gentle cycle, turned inside out in a mesh bag. Smooth out the creases while it is wet and dry it flat, or hung over a thick pole, and it keeps its shape. As with all knitwear, expect a variation of 1–2 cm between pieces. Made in Japan.

product.title: ONI Denim 275 20oz Awa Kakishibu x Kinari Regular Straight Jeans
product.body_html:
This rare collector’s edition from ONI features hand-dyed Awa kakishibu warp yarns and natural undyed (kinari) weft yarns, creating a warm, earthy tone with subtle depth and a soft, organic presence. Kakishibu is a traditional Japanese dye made from fermented persimmon tannin—historically used for textiles, wood, and paper— prized for the way it ages beautifully, darkening and developing character as it oxidizes with sunlight and wears.

The fabric is woven on antique shuttle looms at low tension. The result is a 20oz slubby denim with rich texture and slow, graceful fading that reflects the touch of the craftsperson. The kinari weft adds a natural warmth beneath the kakishibu-dyed warp, giving the denim a quiet, understated complexity that deepens with time and wear.

Cut in the ONI 275 Regular Straight fit, this pair offers a balanced silhouette with a comfortable rise and room throughout—versatile, classic, and easy to wear.

Fit Notes: These jeans have a standard sizing. We recommend choosing your usual size. However, as always, we recommend checking the size chart first to find your perfect size. The fabric is unsanforized, but the jeans have been one-washed, so no further shrinkage is expected. The waist will experience the typical stretching seen in ONI denim due to the low tension weave, although not as much as the secret denim. Expect approximately 1 inches of stretching.

product.title: TCB New Cats Drive Jeans

After about three years, TCB brings the series back, and these are its jeans.

The revival revisits one element: the fabric. TCB kept the EMOT cotton blend of the first run — East Memphis, New Orleans and Texas — but not its yarn. The original was woven with a 5.7-count warp and a 6.7-count weft, engineered for the long, continuous fading lines of left-hand twill; watching that batch age, the brand wanted the streaks longer still. Both warp and weft now sit at a 6-count, and the slubs have been lengthened to build more variation into the surface, so the denim fades in elongated vertical streaks rather than short breaks.

The cut follows the riding logic on the chart: a high rise (12.4" at the front on a 32) that sits at the natural waist, a close thigh and a slim straight leg tapering to a 7.7" opening — proportions made for boots, and for a jacket that closes at the waist.

product.title: TCB 13.5oz Baggy 50’s Jeans
product.body_html:
TCB started with the 50's. Thirteen years ago they were the first jeans the brand made — its first answer to the question of what the best jeans are — and every pair since has been measured against them: wider or slimmer, heavier or lighter, this tinge of indigo or that. When TCB began shipping overseas it drew a Slim 50's for foreign customers, the way Japanese cars are converted to left-hand drive for export. The Baggy 50's comes from the opposite direction. Young staff at TCB had been customizing the 50's pattern and wearing it baggy, and Inoue-san decided it deserved a proper shape — the same instinct that once had mods shrinking jeans in the bath and skaters buying them oversized. One pattern, read by a new generation.

Fabric and sewing specifications are exactly those of the 50's. The denim is approx. 13.5oz, 100% Zimbabwe cotton, woven on a vintage loom rather than a computer-regulated one, so the yarn thickness and tension vary naturally across the cloth. It fades the vintage way: white dots appear first, then join into long vertical lines. What changes is the silhouette — a modern wide cut with plenty of room through the hips, thighs and hem, on a high-set rise (12.2" at the front on a 32), with a slight taper to a 8.9" opening.

The construction is TCB's reproduction work at its most detailed. The paper patch is sewn on by hand, and around the time the fades come good it begins to tear, showing the dark blue beneath. Hidden rivets on the back pockets are attached by the most durable of the many period methods. Sewing thread is 100% cotton in four colors and five yarn counts, with seam widths matched to the vintage piece TCB owns and the vintage machines set up accordingly — down to the pocket bags, which were roughly sewn on the originals and are roughly sewn here, with the durability kept. Designed and made in Kojima, Japan.

That purpose shows in the cut, close through the body and shaped at the waist so nothing bunches in the saddle.

The fabric is where TCB has done the work. The original run used EMOT cotton — a blend drawn from East Memphis, New Orleans and Texas — with a 5.7-count warp and 6.7-count weft, engineered to produce the long, continuous fading lines that left-hand twill is known for. Watching that first batch age, the brand wanted the streaks longer still. So both warp and weft have been moved to a 6-count yarn, and the slubs have been lengthened, physically building more variation into the surface so that the fades run in elongated vertical streaks rather than short breaks. Same cotton, same twill direction, a different result in five years' time.

The yarn is hand dyed with natural indigo harvested from the Tokushima prefecture in Japan. Only a handful of indigo craftsmen are capable of this dyeing technique. It is certified by the Japanese government as a national living treasure.

The lengthy fermenting process required to produce natural indigo and the low annual output make this a highly coveted dye material. The undyed cotton yarns are dipped by hand into indigo dye vats repeatedly until the indigo has penetrated the core of the yarns.

For this reason, natural indigo jeans have a reputation for retaining their color. Most jeans use indigo dyed yarns that are white at the core, since they have not fully absorbed the indigo. The top layer of indigo will eventually give way to the white centers with moderate wear and abrasion. Natural indigo models hold their blue color longer making them tougher to break in, but this adds to their uniqueness.
